articles.title_orig: Nvidia Chinese Spy Story Is Getting Worse: Huang's Affair Helped Move $7.5 Billion in Chips to China - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Chinese Spy Story Is Getting Worse: Huang's Affair Helped Move $7.5 Billion in Chips to China - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
Following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admission on Sunday to an extramarital affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, the chipmaker's relationship to China is about to come under intense scrutiny in Washington, D.C.
Since October 2022, when the Biden administration announced sweeping controls to limit China's ability to obtain advanced U.S. chips, Nvidia has seen its business diminish in the world's second-largest economy. Months after an even stricter set of rules was implemented by the Trump administration, Huang said in October 2025, "We are 100% out of China."
The recent allegations against Huang, while throwing the chipmaker into crisis, have also brought attention to the Nvidia CEO's potential influence over U.S. policy on chip sales to China, where its business once flourished. Of particular interest is whether restricted Nvidia chips have reached Chinese companies through customers like Singapore-based Megaspeed , the company linked to Alice Huang.
The New York Times first reported that the Chinese businesswoman was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, according to people briefed on the intelligence circulated in a memo among the Trump administration in the spring. China has called the allegation a smear.
Jensen Huang has been closely aligned with President Donald Trump during his second administration, helping advise the White House on artificial intelligence safety regulations, while also pushing for looser restrictions on selling AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia would be allowed to ship its H200 chips to China, provided the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales. In March, Huang told reporters that Nvidia had "received purchase orders, and we're in the process of restarting our manufacturing ."
Huang was a last-minute addition to the roster of tech executives who joined Trump on a trip to China in May, after the president was briefed on intelligence concerns, according to the Times .
"In 35 years, I haven't seen a chip CEO with this much direct influence on export policy," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO at Moor Insights & Strategy, in an email.
Since last week's midterm elections that included sweeping victories across the country for Democrats, the mood in Washington has changed. Three House committees have requested closed-door briefings with the Nvidia CEO about his relationship with Megaspeed.
Democratic lawmakers, who are about to take power in the House and Senate, have said publicly that Congress will investigate and seek answers. Trump said Monday that he was "amazed" by the allegations and that Huang told him he "had no idea that she was a spy." The FBI is now looking into the issue, Trump said at a White House briefing.
It's been a long four years for Nvidia in China.
Before the initial export controls in 2022, China made up nearly a quarter of Nvidia's revenue. Nvidia responded to the Biden-era restrictions by redesigning some of its products to comply with the new regulations.
"It was a turbulent month or so as the company went upside down to re-engineer" the products, Huang told CNBC in a 2023 interview. Still, he was confident the company could continue selling chips to China. "I think we're going to be just fine in the ability to serve the customers there," he said.
After the Biden administration tightened export restrictions again, Nvidia redesigned another AI graphics processing unit for China, the H20. Following reports that Chinese model developer DeepSeek was using restricted Nvidia chips, the Trump administration limited sales of H20. Nvidia revealed it would incur $5.5 billion in costs related to canceled orders for the redesigned chip.
However, despite saying in its forecasts that "we're assuming 0% for China," the company maintained business in the region. In the last fiscal year, Nvidia reported that about 9% of its revenue came from China, including Hong Kong, although that includes revenue from segments outside of restricted data center chips, such as gaming, auto and industrial. Nvidia's China revenue was 8% in the most recent quarter.
A report in May from short seller Culper Research alleged Nvidia's China exposure was much higher. The firm said that more than 20% of Nvidia's fiscal 2026 compute revenue was driven by China, supported by "illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries," according to the report.
A loophole allows Chinese companies to rent Nvidia GPUs in data centers, even when they're restricted from buying them outright. For example, a Chinese company could lease Nvidia computing power in Europe by renting server capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that's exempt from export controls.
Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment for this story.
Megaspeed , an Nvidia customer based in Singapore, has been accused of diverting its own supply of Nvidia's restricted AI chips to Chinese companies. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and said inspections found no evidence of violations.
In 2025, Nvidia changed the way it reported regional sales to categorize by customer headquarters, instead of by where the products were billed. Nvidia also stopped reporting Singapore sales during the same period.
"Whether Blackwell chips reached China is a Megaspeed question that predates this week," said Moorhead, pointing to Bloomberg reporting in December 2025 that found Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more Nvidia chips than Nvidia tallied in its data centers.
In 2025, a House Select Committee opened an investigation into whether China's DeepSeek operates on Nvidia's chips.
A separate investigation by the U.S. Commerce Department was centered on Megaspeed. That probe was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department, the Times reported , following an email from Nvidia's general counsel to the Commerce Department seeking information about the investigation.
The restrictions aren't just coming from the U.S. China has continued to limit the amount of Nvidia chips it will allow into the country, keeping Nvidia's China sales numbers down. The U.S. has licensed H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, but Beijing hasn't approved large-scale imports, Moorhead told CNBC. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July.
Moorhead expects more export control legislation to pass as a result of the latest turmoil. Proposals could allow Congress oversight of chip export licenses or require chipmakers to install security mechanisms to track the location of chips to determine if they've found their way to China.
"Every China license now gets read through this story," Moorhead said. "Jensen has been Nvidia's lead voice on China, and that voice is weaker."
— CNBC's Kif Leswing and Seema Mody contributed reporting to this report.
Correction: Three House committees have requested closed-door briefings with the Nvidia CEO about his relationship with Megaspeed. An earlier version misstated the time element.

articles.title_orig: Russia and Ukraine hold nearly 4 hours of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.title_zh: Russia and Ukraine hold nearly 4 hours of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.content_orig:
Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's foreign intelligence service (third from the right), speaks during the coordination meeting before the trilateral talks between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the U.S. in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, Tuesday. Altaf Qadri/Pool AP hide caption
ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Three-way talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates as Washington made another push to end the war that followed Moscow's all-out invasion of its neighbor nearly five years ago.
Hopes of ending Europe's biggest conflict since World War II are tempered by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks earlier this year.
There's nothing to suggest a new posture that would lead to a breakthrough, but circumstances surrounding the talks have been changed by the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections as well as increased pressure on Russia's wartime economy. Moscow also is seeking to break Ukrainians' will as winter sets in by ramping up its battering of the country's power grid.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the nearly four-hour talks were "constructive and quite substantive," and largely were about humanitarian issues, including prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country. Security guarantees also were discussed, he added during an appearance at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark.
Speaking in Paris at the Group of Seven meeting, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the talks were "very productive," but added: "There's a lot of work to be done in that regard."
The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February on the war, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians. A second round is expected Wednesday.
United Arab Emirates Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan sits flanked by Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law (left), and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff during talks between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the U.S. in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, Tuesday. Altaf Qadri/Pool AP hide caption
U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who along with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff is trying to broker a settlement, said he believed there were "some good ideas how to bridge" the differences between the two sides.
Trump, whose stance on the war has varied, must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. elections. Democrats could demand more support for Ukraine.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told ZDF television on Monday night that "I don't have overly high expectations" for the talks.
There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks come against a backdrop of new long-range strikes by both Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.
Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces downed 155 Ukrainian drones overnight in eight Russian regions, as well as over the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014.
Kushner said in opening remarks that the goal of the talks is to "create a new framework and a new understanding building upon the different institutions and understandings of the past."
"We take what's worked, we try to identify what's failed, why we're in this position and hopefully create a new framework that leads us for decades, if not centuries, of peace," he said.
NATO commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who was also present, pointed to "some great progress in the past in a military-to-military dialogue in a trilateral format."
He said that the U.S. delegation looked forward "to working with both sides as we seek to advance the progress we've made in the past and continue this pursuit to set the foundations for a lasting peace."
Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service who leads Kyiv's delegation, thanked the U.S. for its efforts to end Russia's invasion.
"Our people are waiting to end this war. And we hope that we will achieve the lasting peace for Ukraine," he said.
The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, expressed hope the meeting "will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine."
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy walks alongside Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, right, as he arrives at the Danish Parliament Christiansborg, in Copenhagen, Tuesday. Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix via AP hide caption
Umerov said the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission.
The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal.
Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from four regions of Ukraine that Moscow annexed in September 2022 but has never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.
Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.
UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan speaks to U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff during the trilateral talks between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the US in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, Tuesday. Altaf Qadri/Pool AP hide caption
Zelenskyy rejects Putin's demands to voluntarily cede territory. He also rejects any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.
Ukraine argues an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled. Putin has spurned those suggestions.
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.
Russia's chief negotiator is Medinsky, a Putin aide who has led Moscow's team since the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and deputy chief of the General Staff's operational department Yuri Zhigarlovsky.
Besides Umerov, the Ukrainian delegation also reportedly includes Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy, Sergiy Kyslytsya, and Davyd Arakhamia, the parliamentary faction leader of Zelenskyy's Servant of the People party.
Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as "a big agreement" that is "going to involve more than Ukraine."
Kushner said Monday on X that a "comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them."
Moscow has praised the broad approach.
"We can only welcome the (U.S.) negotiators on President Donald Trump's request proposing to put the issue of collective security on top of the agenda of the talks on a Ukrainian settlement," Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
Some in the European Union see Washington's proposals as too accommodating to Moscow.
Russia has objected to the Europeans' involvement in the three-way talks, but said EU representatives could join at a later stage.

articles.content_orig:
China has extended its suspension of the export controls on rare earths, lithium ion batteries and graphite anode materials it announced in October 2025. The extension runs only until 10 January 2027. The original announcement suspended the restrictions for a year.

China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) published the notice on 9 November, a day before the original suspension was due to expire. It gave no reason for the particular length of the extension.

articles.title_zh: 10 PS Plus Extra, Premium Games for November 2026 Announced
articles.content_orig:
Soul Reaver 2 and Freedom Wars  Remastered join PlayStation Plus Premium.
This month, embark on an inspiring mission of human connection in Death Stranding 2: On the Beach, assemble a one-of-a-kind crew as you explore the open sea in Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii, navigate the cult-controlled ruins, natural caves, and nuclear bunkers of a green and unpleasant British countryside in Atomfall, or explore a vast world map with an abundance of captivating locations in Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake. All these titles and more are available in November’s PlayStation Plus Game Catalog lineup*. Meanwhile, Soul Reaver 2 and Freedom Wars Remastered land into PlayStation Plus Premium.
Death Stranding 2: On the Beach | PS5
Embark on an inspiring mission of human connection beyond the UCA. Join Sam for the next chapter of his journey as he attempts to connect Australia to the Chiral Network. Navigate a living environment through day and night cycles, natural disasters including earthquakes, sandstorms and forest fires, and Timefall – a rain that instantly ages everything it touches. To traverse this dangerous landscape, you’ll need to build new types of infrastructure, master specialised equipment, and confront (or evade) the otherworldly creatures that roam the fractured world.
Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii | PS5, PS4
A new legend begins as you step into the steel toe boots of Goro Majima, a man who has lost his memory and reinvents himself as a pirate on the open sea. Embark on an over-the-top, modern-day pirate adventure with an ex-yakuza, now pirate captain and his crew as they engage in exhilarating combat on land and sea in the hunt for lost memories and a legendary treasure.
Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii will be available November 24 in the US, the UK and Japan.
A survival-action game inspired by real-life events, Atomfall is set five years after the Windscale nuclear disaster in Northern England. Explore the fictional quarantine zone, scavenge, craft, barter, fight and talk your way through a British countryside setting filled with bizarre characters, mysticism, cults, and rogue government agencies. From Rebellion, the studio behind Sniper Elite and Zombie Army, Atomfall will challenge you to solve the dark mystery of what really happened.
Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake | PS5
A stunning reimagining of the beloved RPG masterpiece and narrative beginning to The Erdrick Trilogy. Years ago, the great hero Ortega bid farewell to his wife and child as he set off on a quest to defeat the villainous Archfiend, Baramos. Ortega failed his quest, and Baramos still threatens the world. Now, on their 16th birthday, Ortega’s only child is summoned by the king of Aliahan and entrusted with a mission of the highest import: to take on Ortega’s quest, vanquish Baramos and save the world.
In Trepang2, you play as an escaped soldier who has no memories of their past life, but is infused with supernatural abilities. Revenge is on your mind, and you’ll stop at nothing to get what you want. Deliver devastating punches, sneak around in the shadows, wield explosive weapons, and give the bad guys a taste of their own medicine. Fight back, find the truth and face a threat even deadlier than yourself.
Trepang2 will be available November 24 in the US and the UK.
Experience the full intensity of the 2026 MotoGP Championship with all the official riders, teams, bikes and tracks in a more authentic way: for the first time, the real-world results dynamically update Riders Ratings, directly influencing in-game performance throughout the season. Step into the spotlight and track your journey with dazzling Collectible Cards celebrating your progress.
MotoGP 26 will be available November 24 in the US and the UK.
Join the ever-expanding experience of Hell Let Loose – a hardcore World War Two first person shooter with epic battles of 100 players with infantry, tanks, artillery, a dynamically shifting front line and a unique resource based RTS-inspired meta-game. Take to the battlefield in 50 vs 50 multiplayer across huge maps. Choose one of 14 playable roles within infantry, recon and armour unit types, each equipped with different weapons, vehicles and equipment. Play as an Officer, Scout, Machine Gunner, Medic, Engineer, Tank Commander and more to experience every aspect of World War II combat.
Hell Let Loose will be available tomorrow, November 11 in the US, the UK and November 12 in Japan.
Cricket 26 – The Official Game of the Ashes | PS5, PS4
Featuring the all-new Management Career, a bigger and better Pro Team, in-depth Ashes mode, and expanded control on and off the field from enhanced gameplay and in-depth strategies – Cricket 26 is The Ultimate Showdown.
Cricket 26 – The Official Game of the Ashes will be available November 24 in the US and the UK.
Soul Reaver 2 | PS5, PS4 In this sequel to the critically acclaimed Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver, reassume the role of Raziel, and battle back through the currents of time into pivotal, dangerous eras of Nosgoth’s past in your relentless pursuit of Kain. Encounter new enemies as you unearth the mysteries of Nosgoth’s ancient races, and expose the schemes that lie behind the corruption of the Pillars.
Freedom Wars Remastered | PS5, PS4
In a distant future where all resources on earth have been depleted, being alive is a sin by itself. Born into a one-million-year prison sentence, you must survive deadly missions to earn any hope of freedom. Die in prison or live on the battlefield. The choice is yours. Use your most trusted weapon, your Thorn, to dominate the battlefield. Stand alongside your allies and your warden cyborg Accessory to face off against powerful enemies.
*PlayStation Plus Game Catalog and PlayStation Plus Premium/Deluxe lineups may differ by region. Please check PlayStation Store on release day. Digital PS5 games available to stream from your library will vary over time, region, and country.

PlayStation believes in providing high-quality experiences to our players, and we regularly review offerings to ensure we are focusing on experiences our members value most. With a very small number of eligible PlayStation Plus Premium members (less than 0.4%) using the PlayStation Plus app on PC, making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use. Shelves were left bare by the cyber-attacks
Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as "baseless and hostile".
On Monday, the French authorities blamed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for the string of hacks, which foreign minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot said were "unprecedented" in terms of their scale and "level of aggression".
He added that those responsible would be hit with sanctions.
The French cyber-attacks, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food, were followed by a similar hacks against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
On Monday, some Iranian media outlets denied the French accusations, but there had been no official comment until Tuesday's statement from Iran's foreign ministry.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of CoopÃ©rative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.
Additional reporting by Farshad Bayan, BBC Persian.

articles.content_orig:
iPadOS 27.3 is currently available in beta , and it introduces a new iPad setting for app windowing that I instantly turned on. Here are the details.
I use the iPad Pro as my primary computer, and for the most part have found Apple’s software changes in iPadOS 26 and 27 to be great upgrades.
But with the powerful new windowing capabilities, there have definitely been some quirks that need refining. One of them involves resizing windows with the traffic light controls in the top-left corner.
For example, in iPadOS 27 the controls move locations and even disappear depending on the size of the window. It can be pretty frustrating.
I need to just get better about learning keyboard shortcuts for window controls. But in the meantime, iPadOS 27.3 adds a new optional setting that I instantly turned on and have been loving.
Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if you have ‘Windowed Apps’ enabled you’ll see a new option below it: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom’
If you use your iPad mostly with touch input, or simply haven’t used keyboard shortcuts enough to remember them, this new setting is a great way to quickly resize windows.
When the setting is enabled, two taps (or a double-click with the trackpad) will zoom the window to take up the full screen. Then you can double-tap again to revert it to its previous size.
I generally keep my app windows in specific size setups, but regularly find myself wanting to go fullscreen temporarily. The new setting provides a convenient way to do that quickly without needing the traffic light controls or my keyboard, and is a welcome refinement to iPadOS windowing.

NEW YORK, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Oil prices slid about 2% to fresh two-month lows on Tuesday after US officials downplayed the need for additional military action against Iran, easing fears of additional Middle East supply disruptions.
Brent futures fell $1.93, or 2.1%, to $90.64 a barrel at 10:28 a.m. ‌ET (1528 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell $1.44, or 1.7%, to $85.41.
That put both crude benchmarks on track for their lowest closes since August 28. On ‌Monday, both contracts closed at their lowest since August 31.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that he told Group of Seven allies that the US economic sanctions and naval blockade are working so ​well that US President Donald Trump does not need to conduct major combat operations in Iran.
Rubio made the comments during a meeting in Paris of foreign ministers from the G7, which comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, as well as the European Union.
On Monday, Trump said he plans to hold off on new military strikes against Iran for the time being after appeals from countries in the region, including from Qatar's prime minister in White House talks.
"The market continues to prioritize President Trump's more conciliatory tone toward ‌Iran since the midterms," said Tim Waterer, chief market ⁠analyst at KCM Trade.
In last week's US midterm elections, voters focused on the rising cost of living, which was fueled by Republican Trump's trade tariffs and higher energy costs from the war with Iran, and handed solid majorities in both houses of Congress to the ⁠Democratic Party.
Trump, in a Reuters interview and a later appearance in the White House press briefing room, said he plans to keep up a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz for now. Before the US and Israel started attacking Iran in February, about 20% of the world's oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
More than eight months into the conflict, ​Trump ​has played down the likelihood of major warfare restarting soon but remains unwilling to accept an ​existing Iranian truce plan. Senior US and Gulf officials have cast ‌doubt on the chances of an imminent deal.
Mutual attacks continue, with the US striking Iran's Qeshm island overnight, according to Iranian state media, and Iran attacking tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz this month while its Yemeni Houthi allies have hit Saudi Arabia.
Russian and Ukrainian officials met in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their first peace talks since February as Trump's envoys launched a new push to end the war in Ukraine.
The US-brokered meeting followed US contacts with both sides in recent weeks, which Trump's representative Jared Kushner said had narrowed the gaps between their positions.
Rubio described the meeting as very productive, without giving details.
Despite US optimism, the warring sides remain far ‌apart on terms for a possible settlement, more than 4-1/2 years after Russia's full-scale invasion ​of Ukraine. Russia controls about a fifth of its neighbor's territory.
Russia was the world's third-biggest crude oil ​producer behind the US and Saudi Arabia in 2025, US energy data showed. ​Sanctions designed to keep Russian energy out of global markets after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine have helped support oil prices.
Any deal to ‌end Russia's invasion of Ukraine could allow Russia to export more.
In a move that could reduce future ​oil demand, investors said the release of data on Tuesday showing US consumer prices increased by more than expected in October made it more likely the US Federal Reserve would raise interest rates half a percentage point at its December meeting.
A strong jobs market, resilient economic growth and inflation stuck above the Fed's ​2% target for nearly six years all suggest further tightening ‌is required.
Central banks, like the Fed, use interest rates to control inflation. Higher interest rates raise consumer costs, which can reduce economic growth and ​demand for oil.

articles.title_orig: Changes are coming to Social Security in January — here’s what Americans should know
articles.title_zh: Changes are coming to Social Security in January — here’s what Americans should know
articles.content_orig:
Starting in January, Social Security recipients will see two major changes.
The Social Security Administration (SSA) — a program providing financial benefits to eligible workers after reaching retirement age — will increase benefits and taxes. Back in October, the SSA announced that recipients will see a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) .
The COLA is the yearly increase meant to help Social Security keep up with rising prices.
This means nearly 72 million retirees will most likely see their Social Security benefits increase by about $75 per month starting in January. The increased payments will hit roughly 7.3 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) beginning on December 31, 2026.
Another change to hit millions of beneficiaries — some added taxes. Based on increases in average wages, the maximum amount of income subject to Social Security will increase next year.
For example, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax — known as taxable maximum — is set to increase from $184,500 to $192,300 in 2027.
The move will impact higher earners, as many will soon start paying Social Security taxes on an additional $7,800 in reported income. For example, someone earning at least $192,300 would likely pay up to $483.60 more annually in Social Security taxes.
The agency has recently announced another revision — the biggest change in its 91-year history . The SSA revealed it has officially “cleaned up” the comprehensive Social Security Number (SSN) database.
SSA records are referenced by federal government agencies and in states to validate identities — which helps prevent improper payments of taxpayer dollars. While it may seem like a small, administrative change, the move safeguards identity data, helps to prevent fraud and preserves proper program administration.
According to the office, it added 17 million dates of death to records that previously lacked this information, updated about 25 million records that previously had missing citizenship information and more.
For most recipients, it’s business as usual. No Social Security numbers have been taken; your monthly checks are still coming and recipients will still see a COLA bump.
To view your COLA notice online, head to your Social Security account. If you receive paperless notices, you may view and save your COLA notice in the “Message Center” starting in late November.
However, you must create an online “my Social Security account” and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see yours online. The agency will send paper notices with updated benefit amounts in early December.
And don’t forget — you may see an early Social Security check as Veterans Day falls on a Wednesday.

articles.title_zh: Trump’s Board of Peace chides Israel for ‘insufficient’ response to Gaza flooding
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace urged Israel to allow essential aid into Gaza, after calling its response to massive weekend flooding across the shattered enclave “insufficient.”
Seasonal rains swamped tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, where nearly 2 million Palestinians are displaced, according to the United Nations.
“The urgent entry and distribution of essential shelter, sanitation, drainage, and other winterization supplies is critical to protecting civilian lives,” the Board of Peace said in a statement Monday.
Created by the Trump administration and backed by a UN Security Council resolution, the organization was supposed to oversee implementation of a Gaza ceasefire signed a year ago, and the reconstruction of the enclave, but the effort has stalled for months.
The Board of Peace called on Israel to “authorize the entry of essential materials for temporary shelter, water and sanitation infrastructure, waste management, drainage, and sewage removal.” Much of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed in Israel’s bombardment of the territory during three years of war.
Trump says ‘great dislike’ for Israel contributed to Republican midterm losses
Since the nominal ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, Israel’s near-daily strikes have killed more than 1,400 people in Gaza, according to the UN, and no hospitals in the enclave are fully functioning.
Philippe Lazzarini, the former head of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), described the board’s assessment of the Israeli response to the floods as an “understatement.” Lazzarini noted its “rare recognition” that Israel is not doing enough to address the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, then slammed the board – which largely avoids harsh criticism of the Israeli government – saying “it does not use any of its leverage to address the disgraceful dystopian misery of the Palestinians in Gaza.”
On Sunday evening, a sand embankment in Deir al-Balah collapsed on the tents of displaced Palestinians after heavy rains, killing three children and one woman, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who led a multinational effort to impose sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, warned, “The humanitarian situation in Gaza is getting worse. Heavy rain. Flooded tents. The reality on the ground is heartbreaking.”
“The UK government will not standby. We will not rest until we bring an end to the intolerable suffering,” he said in a statement on X.
On Sunday, Israel said that more than 91,000 tents had entered Gaza ahead of winter, but it will not allow in the heavy equipment required for large-scale cleanup and rubble removal efforts.
“The reconstruction of Gaza can only begin after Hamas fully disarms,” said Israel’s Coordinator for Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), which oversees Gaza. “Israel will not permit the entry of equipment that could be used to develop terrorist capabilities.”

Apple’s HomeView arrives this Friday ( pre-order here ), but leaks indicate there are already two major new features in the works that haven’t been announced. Here’s what to expect.
It’s been a busy product launch season for Apple, and the company isn’t done quite yet.
Two new Home products arrive in stores this Friday, November 13: Apple HomeView and the new Apple TV 4K .
Yet despite the HomeView still being days away from launch, leaks in Apple code have already revealed two unannounced features that are in the works.
Leaker pdfu discovered evidence in HomeView 27.2 software that Apple is preparing for the product to add security camera functionality.
Apple HomeView could soon double as a HomeKit security camera. The feature has concrete settings localization in HomeView Software 27.2, describing functionality and privacy protections. Here are the exact localization strings: Setup Page Your HomeView can be used as a… pic.twitter.com/NsnknajWKd
Based on pdfu’s findings, much of the work has already been done for HomeView to integrate with HomeKit Secure Video.
However, Apple hasn’t announced any sort of security camera functionality, so there’s clearly still more work to be done and it’s always possible the feature is never enabled.
Additionally, pdfu found a key change in iOS 27.3’s beta that reveals support for third-party AI apps is coming to HomeView.
HomeView has a unique third-party app story. There’s no App Store, but the product can run CarPlay-compatible apps from your iPhone automatically. At launch, only audio and video apps will be supported.
But iOS 27.3’s beta code adds “conversational apps” as a third category of supported apps. That’s what AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude are classified as in CarPlay.
Nobody should buy a HomeView in the hope of these two features being added. But if you are interested in HomeView, it sounds like Apple has an ambitious set of software updates planned for its new product.

Rockstar Games is making Grand Theft Auto VI available on Xbox Cloud Gaming when it launches next week. While you’d normally assume that would mean Grand Theft Auto VI would be available to stream on phones, PCs, the web, Xbox consoles, and even TVs, it appears to be restricted to just Xbox Series X / S and Xbox One consoles.
That does mean that anyone with an older Xbox One console can stream Grand Theft Auto VI instead of having to upgrade to a PS5 or Xbox Series S / X console to play. Rockstar notes that Xbox Cloud Gaming will use the Xbox Series S graphics settings to stream to Xbox consoles.
Xbox’s own announcement blog post only mentions Xbox Cloud Gaming streaming for Xbox Series X / S and Xbox One owners. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma says the cloud deal for Grand Theft Auto VI is “the first step in our new 10-year strategic partnership with Take-Two.” Sharma also says the game is “the most pre-ordered game ever on Microsoft Store.” Microsoft is also planning to add Grand Theft Auto V , Red Dead Redemption 2 , and more to Xbox Cloud Gaming in “the coming months.”
What this all means is that Microsoft effectively has an exclusive on streaming Grand Theft Auto VI from the cloud for launch, albeit only to Xbox consoles.
I originally reported last month that Microsoft had secured exclusive Grand Theft Auto VI cloud streaming rights, but Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball revealed on X that Microsoft wouldn’t be streaming Grand Theft Auto VI exclusively. While Microsoft’s contract might not specifically state exclusive, the end result is exclusive cloud gaming on Xbox, for now. Sony may well eventually announce its own cloud streaming plans for the game, but Rockstar Games notes that Grand Theft Auto VI “will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox.” That’s not cloud streaming, though.
I also initially reported that Grand Theft Auto VI would be available to stream on PC, simply because the entire point of Xbox Cloud Gaming is to make games available on Xbox consoles, TVs, PCs, and the web. It’s strange to see a rare exception for Grand Theft Auto VI , but not entirely surprising. Perhaps Microsoft will eventually be able to stream the PC version of Grand Theft Auto VI whenever it launches.

articles.title_orig: 'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
articles.title_zh: 'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
articles.content_orig:
FILE - In this photo provided by the North Korean government, its leader Kim Jong Un, center, and his daughter, reportedly named Kim Ju Ae, visit a military training base in North Korea, Thursday, March 19, 2026. Independent journalists were not given access to cover the event depicted in this image distributed by the North Korean government. The content of this image is as provided and cannot be independently verified. 朝鮮通信社/KCNA via KNS via AP hide caption
SEOUL, South Korea — Until she fled North Korea three years ago, Kim Yumi felt deeply frustrated whenever state TV showed leader Kim Jong Un with his young daughter. The message, she felt, was clear and worrying: North Korea was laying the groundwork for an eventual hereditary transfer of power, this time to Kim's daughter.
Publicly questioning the Kim dynasty's hold on power would mean severe persecution. Already angered by draconian pandemic regulations that ruined her family's fishing business, she defected to South Korea by boat with her family.
"My husband and I didn't want our children to live under a fourth-generation dictatorship. As parents, we thought the best thing we could do for our children was to give them freedom," said Kim Yumi, 32, who now lives in Seoul.
North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty, with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession. There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions — from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011.
This time, North Korea is apparently trying something radical.
Kim Jong Un's repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years have led to speculation that she's being groomed as her father's heir.
The question of who will become North Korea's next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge — governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.
North Koreans have no say in the selection of their future leader, and analysts and defectors say they will passively accept a third dynastic succession — at least publicly.
To gauge North Koreans' private views, The Associated Press spoke with nearly a dozen defectors who still have contacts in North Korea or witnessed the country's previous power successions, as well as several experts.
Not much is known about Kim's daughter except that she's reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae.
Since late 2022, she has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim's "most beloved" and "respected" child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father.
South Korea's spy agency says she is Kim's likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by the AP shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North's deeply patriarchal culture.
"During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un," said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea's Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. "They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un," when he accompanied his father as his heir.
Tae Yongho, a former minister of North Korea's Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016, speaks during an interview with The Associated Press in Seoul, South Korea, Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Lee Jin-man/AP hide caption
Kang Mi-Jin, a defector who runs a company analyzing North Korea's economy, said her contacts inside the North told her over smuggled phones that they think Kim Ju Ae is in line to succeed her father.
Jung Gwang-il, a defector who specializes in smuggling outside information to North Korea, said the North Koreans he meets as they visit Chinese border towns also hold the same belief.
Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity, holding her as a baby during a 2013 trip to Pyongyang.
Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn't been confirmed.
Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers' Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un's influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry.
"My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader," said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009.
Lee Si-young, a defector who heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station, said that some of her older contacts in North Korea aren't happy with a woman taking power. But she said members of the Kim family "are like gods reigning over humans so gender really doesn't matter."
Whether or not the girl succeeds her father, observers agree that Kim Jong Un, 42, is likely to designate one of his children to prolong his family's rule, a move they expect would face little resistance at home. South Korea's spy agency recently assessed that Kim is extremely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease but shows no other signs of poor health.
North Koreans will passively "accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with," said Ahn Chan-il, a defector and scholar who heads the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul.
During North Korea's first leadership transition, in 1994, the new leader, Kim Jong Il, then 52, had already spent two decades as the official successor working alongside his father to run the country.
The second succession, in 2011, was more uncertain. Kim Jong Un, who was then 27, was seen by outsiders as too young and inexperienced. He quickly consolidated his grip on power, however, by orchestrating high-profile executions and purges, including the 2013 killing of his powerful uncle Jang Song Thaek.
"A hereditary power succession system has been institutionalized in North Korea, just like presidential elections in our system," said Oh Gyeong-seob, an analyst at Seoul's Korea Institute for National Unification. "North Korea's ruling elite accepts it as a matter of course. So do its general citizens."
Choi Song-juk, who fled North Korea in 2015, said she had been so brainwashed that she had no complaints about the North's two earlier power successions. She now calls them "nonsense."
Defector Jeon Jae-hyun said North Korea's pervasive surveillance apparatus keeps people from voicing their discontent with the government and helps enforce political loyalty.
Defector Kim Yumi said she had never heard about the girl until Kim Jong Un publicly introduced his daughter at a long-range missile launch site in November 2022.
"Ordinary people know absolutely nothing about private lives of the Kim family," said Kim Yumi, who now runs a YouTube channel on North Korea. "They don't really try to know about it and don't pay attention to it because doing so could put them in danger."

Adobe is pouring more AI into its products, including Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, and InDesign, in a major product feature announcement at its MAX event in Miami. The company is also expanding AI capabilities in its creative tool, Firefly, and releasing a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that lets other chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini use Adobe features.
Adobe’s Firefly app is moving into Figma’s territory with a new prototyping tool in private beta called Builder, which lets users create designs to show off ideas. There is also a new tool to create on-brand graphs, along with an image editing tool that lets you change part of an image without changing other objects.
A new AI-powered video tool in Firefly will allow users to assemble a video from clips and other elements like images and sound effects. The company is making its agent proactive and always on so that it can get more context about work and be present for any action. Adobe is also making it easier for people to take quick action, like removing the background or generating a thumbnail for a video.
The company has already added a ton of AI features across its apps like Photoshop, Express, Premiere, and Illustrator . At the MAX event, Adobe is continuing the trend. Photoshop is getting a new relighting feature and sliders for prompt-based generative styles; Premiere will have a new color grading system for professionals and an object removal feature for video; and Lightroom has a way to correct blinking eyes and a blemish removal tool.
Adobe already offers a lot of third-party models from companies like Google, Runway, ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs, OpenAI, Kling, and ByteDance. One of its newer acquisitions, Topaz Labs , is releasing two image models, called Wonder 4 for upscaling and denoising, and ImageHDR, to turn standard images into HDR.
The company already has ChatGPT and Claude integrations to let users access some of its product functions. Now, Adobe is releasing a local MCP to expose more features of its Creative Cloud apps to users.
Adobe vice president Deepa Subramaniam told TechCrunch that the company is still figuring out what capabilities to expose and will rely on user feedback.
“We are still figuring out where and when and how to draw the line. What we’re putting out there is a number of endpoints and capabilities across Illustrator, Photoshop, After Effects, and Premiere. We’re just going to see how people use it, what they’re trying to do, and keep showing more. We don’t have any need or desire to sort of limit what the MCP endpoint can expose. What we really want to do is to support that creative workflow, how you choose to do it,” said Subramaniam.
Last month, Adobe rival Figma co-founder Dylan Field said at an event in India that MCP is not a perfect standard and benefits frontier labs more .

articles.content_orig:
FILE - Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, left, walks with President Prabowo Subianto after Subianto delivered his State of the Nation Address at the parliament building in Jakarta, Indonesia, Friday, Aug. 14, 2026. Dita Alangkara/AP hide caption
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.
Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.
It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to "continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents," Hadi said.
As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.
"I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place," Raka said. "I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy."
The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.
Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.
The developments come amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo. The popular former president backed Prabowo's presidential bid after he chose Raka as a running mate.
The controversy over Raka's academic qualifications escalated last month after the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements.
The ruling intensified political pressure on Raka and fueled calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment.
Widodo faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

articles.title_orig: Iran rejects French claims it was behind supermarket fridge hacking
articles.title_zh: Iran rejects French claims it was behind supermarket fridge hacking
articles.content_orig:
Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as "baseless and hostile".
On Monday, the French authorities blamed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for the string of hacks, which foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said were "unprecedented" in terms of their scale and "level of aggression".
He added that those responsible would be hit with sanctions.
The French cyber-attacks, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food, were followed by a similar hacks against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
On Monday, some Iranian media outlets denied the French accusations, but there had been no official comment until Tuesday's statement from Iran's foreign ministry.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.
Additional reporting by Farshad Bayan, BBC Persian.

articles.title_orig: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses
articles.title_zh: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses
articles.content_orig:
Amazon 's Ring is going deeper into surveillance with an indoor drone for home monitoring and an autonomous robot designed to patrol businesses.
The company on Tuesday unveiled the $250 Ring Drone Cam, a security camera that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, as well as capture footage during the day or at night. When an alarm or sensor on windows, doors and home security devices is triggered, the textbook-sized drone travels a pre-set path to investigate suspicious activity. Users can also deploy the drone at any time, the company said.
At a demo in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff said the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime "deterrent" due to the device's built-in LED lights.
"If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window," Siminoff said. "You're probably not going to go into that house."
The drone, which can fly up to eight minutes at a time before autonomously returning to its charging dock, has two plastic-encased propellers that emit a loud buzz when it's airborne.
Ring devices have provided Amazon another avenue to grow its presence in the smart home beyond its Echo smart speakers and Eero routers, expanding in a market that Grand View Research estimates will top $200 billion in sales this year. It's equally fertile ground for Amazon rivals Apple and Google .
Ring, which Amazon acquired in 2018 and is known for its doorbells, has been beset with privacy concerns , primarily due to its partnerships with police. Earlier this year, Ring faced renewed scrutiny over a controversial Super Bowl ad touting an AI pet-finding tool called "Search Party." It then canceled an integration with police tech provider Flock Safety , which has also faced widespread backlash over its automated license plate readers.
Ring first previewed its drone, then called the Always Home Cam , in 2020. Siminoff said he chose to hold off on releasing the device until Amazon could perfect the design, sensors and data processing.
The company on Tuesday also debuted the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam. The device repurposes Amazon's Astro home robot , which had a short life as a business device and has seen few upgrades since its 2021 debut, for companies to patrol offices, warehouses and other workspaces.
Ring said it "leveraged the best of Astro" to build the Ring Rover Cam, which it describes as a "purpose-built security robot."
Similar to the Astro, the device is a display mounted on a two-wheeled base with an extendable periscope camera. It also features a "built-in siren," two-way audio and a "light tower" that shines onto the ceiling to help users keep track of its whereabouts.
Siminoff said in an interview that the drone and the robot allow users to monitor multiple areas of their home or business with just one device.
"People like indoor cameras, but they don't necessarily want them everywhere around their home," Siminoff said.
Ring said privacy is the "default" mode for both the drone and the robot, which flash an LED light when they're recording.
Siminoff said the drone can't fly outside per Federal Aviation Administration regulations, which restrict operating drones unless they're within a line of sight of a pilot.
"We have told our customers not to do that because it's illegal," Siminoff said. "We've also put guardrails in there to make it so it doesn't fly outside."
The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said.

articles.title_orig: The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
articles.title_zh: The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
articles.content_orig:
Ford Motor vehicles are displayed for sale at the Leif Johnson Ford dealership on June 30 in Austin, Texas. Brandon Bell/Getty Images hide caption
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
The average transaction cost for a new vehicle has reached a record high: $51,109. That's according to a report out today from the Kelley Blue Book, which is part of the analytics firm Cox Automotive.
That's about $500 above the last record , set in December 2025.
Car prices have been stubbornly high for years, especially since the pandemic, mainly driven by supply chain issues. And they've gotten higher recently, in part thanks to tariffs and to buyers flocking to, and car companies making, larger, fancier vehicles.
Yet there's a little good news: Cars are getting more expensive … more slowly .
While that $51,109 figure is an all-time high, that's only up 2.1% in the past year.
"A 2.1% year-over-year increase is actually below inflation," said Erin Keating, an executive analyst at Cox Automotive who co-authored the report. Between 2012 and 2021, cars got 3.4% more expensive a year on average, she continued.
The Kelley Blue Book's transaction cost is based on what people wound up paying for a new vehicle — that means whatever's on the sticker price, plus add-ons for fancier features, and minus any incentives, such as dealer discounts.
It also doesn't include one other expense that adds to the cost of owning a car: interest on auto loans. The cost of borrowing has risen over the past several years as the Federal Reserve has kept interest rates high in an effort to drive down inflation. Auto loan rates are now about 11% for used vehicles and over 7% for new ones, according to Edmunds , a car analytics company.
Keating says all of this can add up to some sticker shock for buyers — partly because people don't buy cars all that often and can be surprised by how expensive they've gotten, and partly because of interest rates.
"I mean, we are seeing a true shift in the percentage of your monthly payment that's going towards interest versus towards principal," she said.
The Kelley Blue Book's average includes all kinds of vehicles — SUVs, pickup trucks, electric vehicles — from all kinds of auto companies, including Toyota, Subaru, Tesla and Mercedes-Benz.
It doesn't, however, include used car sales, which normally make up about two-thirds of total sales. Ivan Drury, director of industry insights at Edmunds, crunched those numbers too and found the same trend. "No matter what you're looking at, the price is up," he said.
The average used car now costs close to $27,000, 6% higher than last year, according to Cox Automotive . Vehicles that cost less than that are a "sliver" of the industry, Drury said.
Supply chain challenges, including a semiconductor shortage, during the COVID pandemic meant fewer cars got made. Carmakers had to pick and choose which vehicles to prioritize making — they picked their most profitable models. As a result, fewer used vehicles entered car lots in the early 2020s. So today there's less inventory to choose from.
That's good for people who already own a car, Drury said. It means people can upgrade to a new car without much additional money up front.
But, he continued, "The consumer that I sympathize with the absolute most? The first-time car buyer." Those buyers face a steep down payment, with nothing to trade in.
No matter whether buyers are choosing new or used, data from Edmunds shows that in 2026, they have been financing with lower down payments and longer auto term lengths. "We've just seen those explode," Drury said.
A report from Edmunds found that car buyers financed more than ever, taking out loans worth an average of $44,664 in the past quarter. They also found that more than a quarter of car buyers financed using loans with 84-month-long terms — or longer.
The combination of a small down payment — sometimes in the range of $500 or $1,000 — and a lengthy loan term can get really expensive for buyers in the long term, Drury said, especially with high interest rates.
"So people just say, 'Oh, forget it,' you know. 'I'll just, I'll just choose the longer term length and put less money down. I've got other bills that are pulling at me,'" Drury said.
In part, vehicles cost more because the cost of making them has gone up for automakers. There are now more tariffs on steel and aluminum, as well as on goods imported from Canada. That matters for American automakers who assemble vehicles on both sides of the border. The cost of computer chips (used in sensors and electronics) and copper (used for automotive wiring) has also risen thanks to competing demand from data centers.
But vehicles also cost more because Americans like bigger cars, SUVs and trucks, which tend to come with a higher price tag. The average sticker price for a full-size pickup truck is nearly $72,000, according to the Kelley Blue Book.
American carmakers have largely shifted their gears away from compact sedans. In earnings calls with investors, they've often cited American demand for bigger vehicles.
Plus, as analyst Mike Wall at Mobility Global points out, smaller vehicles offer lower margins for carmakers. "They were sort of that loss leader. It gets the eyeballs in the door," he said.
For the carmakers, they're not making as much money as they would compared to their bigger vehicles with pricier features.
Drury notes, people appreciate those features. They've gotten used to driving with 360-degree cameras, heated seats and parking assist systems. All of these drive up the cost of buying. "No one wants entry-level anymore," he said. "Everybody goes mid-to-upper trim levels."
"People love walking up to their car that already has the air conditioner going when it's 110 degrees outside, and think, 'You know what? I don't have to get in here and potentially burn my hands,'" Drury continued. "So as we get accustomed to more features, more options, we naturally kind of pile on, too. And automakers, they're very aware of that."
Over the past few years, "automakers have been under incredible stress," Keating said. Yes, there are tariffs and other rising production costs. Many also poured money into developing electric vehicle technology, but EVs still only make up a small slice of the U.S. car market. About 6% of new cars sold are electric, according to Edmunds.
And the market for car buyers is smaller . About 16 million people buy new cars every year — about 1 million fewer since the pandemic.
Notably, fewer people in their late 30s and early 40s are buying cars. "They're just simply holding onto their cars longer," Keating said. Her hypothesis? "That age group and that cohort is simply just dealing with different household pressures for their money and are making the choice to stay in the vehicles that they have."
For the most part, the people buying new cars tend to be older and wealthier. Keating said that might be because older drivers are staying on the road longer. " We have seen this interesting shift towards individuals keeping their licenses longer and therefore more 65 and up, 75 and up individuals are purchasing vehicles than ever before," she said.
For automakers, a drop in car buyers means they have to compete more with each other for sales.
"At the end of the day, each of these competitors are sharing, trying to go after a pie that isn't necessarily growing," Keating said. So instead, " they're stealing share from their competitors as opposed to counting on more consumers entering the picture."

articles.title_zh: Scoop: El Salvador blasts U.S. State Dept. over Haiti gang war
articles.content_orig:
El Salvador's efforts to combat gangs in Haiti brought a rebuke from a U.S. diplomat despite President Trump openly supporting El Salvador.
According to Axios, a diplomatic note was sent to El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, criticizing El Salvador's military efforts in Haiti and said they needed to coordinate with the United Nations-supported Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
"His attitude was, 'What the f*ck? I checked with Trump. He said do what we have to do, and some bureaucrat is fighting this?'" a source who spoke with Bukele told Axios.
Haiti has a weak government and has been battling with gangs since 2020, particularly since the killing of President Jovenel Moïse in 2021. The UN adopted a resolution authorizing the deployment of the GSF in September 2025. It conducts military and intelligence-led operations across Haiti, including beyond Port-au-Prince. The GSF coordinates with the Haitian National Police and the Armed Forces of Haiti.
El Salvador entered the fray after four Salvadoran aviation technicians attached to the GSF were ambushed by gang members on Oct. 18. It is believed the men were kidnapped.
In response, Bukele sent more than 2,500 Salvadoran troops into Haiti — a contingent that was larger than the 1,500-member GSF already deployed.
"Our only goal," he stated at the time, "is to bring our four aviation technicians back home."
Bukele's actions were supported publicly by President Trump, who told Bukele "do what you have to do."
According to Axios, tensions between the State Department and El Salvador flared after an Oct. 31 gang attack. A Salvadoran convoy was fired upon, and the U.S. embassy was struck by gunfire during the clash.
The outlet noted that U.S. Chargé d'Affaires David Howell sent a to Haitian officials complaining that El Salvador wasn't "coordinating" with the GSF. In the message, Howell reportedly told El Salvadoran officials they should stop their activities "as soon as possible ... until they coordinate. They are going to kill [GSF] troops or civilians and or get themselves killed."

articles.title_zh: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
articles.content_orig:
Solange Alexandre twice turned down the LÃ©gion d'Honneur before relenting in 2024
One of France's last Resistance heroes from World War Two has died at the age of 104.  Solange Alexandre was also a rare woman who, with her future husband, created and commanded her own unit of anti-German fighters.
After serving as a Resistance courier from 1941, three years later she founded the Pas-de-Boeuf network near the town of RuillÃ©-sur-Loir.
With some 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and, after the Allied landings in Normandy on D-Day in 1944, joined the fight against the occupying German forces.
President Emmanuel Macron was among many to pay tribute to Alexandre, after her death was announced at a nursing home in Le Mans.
"She said she only ever did her duty. But her duty was our freedom. France will never forget. Thank you," Macron posted on social media.
Born in 1922 in the Sarthe department of western France,  Solange Alexandre, nÃ©e Dubuisson, grew up in a patriotic family that had suffered in World War One.
"My mother lost her first husband in the war, and my father was wounded in 1917.   The words homeland and honour were very important to us. They were in my blood," she recalled in her memoirs.
In June 1940 she heard on the radio the appeal from General Charles de Gaulle in London, calling on the French not to give up the struggle against Germany.  She had never heard of him, but that did not matter.
"From that moment I knew I had to join up," she wrote.
Some months later she was recruited by a friend of her father's â a Tunisian-born French army veteran called SaÃ¯d Belhaffaf, who had joined the Resistance.
Using the code-name Corlay, she criss-crossed the region around Le Mans by bicycle, gathering information and passing on messages.
"There were no mobile phones back then, and no private cars either because of the lack of petrol. The bicycle was king," she said in an interview two years ago.
In 1943 she met her first husband Guy DÃ©liot, who had deserted from the French gendarmerie after refusing to arrest some Jews.
The following April, with the Allied invasion approaching, they decided to take to the maquis, in other words live clandestinely in the forested hills, supplied with food by local farmers.
Their group consisted of deserters from German forced labour programmes, as well as survivors from another Resistance outfit that had been destroyed by the enemy.  There were also two airmen, one American and one Canadian.
"Twice the Gestapo came for me, and twice I slipped through their hands," she later recalled.
After taking part in the liberation of Tours in September 1944, she ended the war with the rank of sub-lieutenant in the French Interior Forces (FFI).
Later she worked as a teacher and followed her husband on his many postings as an officer of the gendarmerie in French overseas territories. He was killed in 1960 in Martinique, and in 1981 she remarried.
Twice Solange Alexandre turned down the LÃ©gion d'Honneur , saying that she had only done her duty and that others were more worthy.
Finally in 2024 she relented.
On receiving the award she said: "It is a great pleasure and a great honour.  I am very proud â even if it is only a few weeks, or a few months, before I die."
